title: Attar turns up the volume as Moore turns out for Ruff, in political notes
summary: Sen. Dalya Attar has her own theme song -- you read that right -- and pumped up the volume and Gov. Wes Moore came out to stump for her opponent, the man behind Eric's ID law gets behind Wanika Fisher, in political notes.
content:
by Christine Condon and William J. Ford, Maryland Matters June 23, 2026

by Christine Condon and William J. Ford, Maryland Matters June 23, 2026

As Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) delivered a stump speech for Del. Malcolm Ruff (D-Baltimore City) on Tuesday in Baltimore, loud music suddenly filled the rainy afternoon air.

It was a theme song for Ruff’s opponent, Sen. Dalya Attar (D-Baltimore City), who was campaigning just a few feet away.

“Baltimore, let’s make it clear: Dalya’s work is what we need here,” a man’s voice sang over a loudspeaker. “Vote Dalya Attar, vote Dalya Attar.”

It was a tense afternoon outside of the polling place at the Forest Park Senior Center in Northwest Baltimore, where the two candidates — both attorneys, both currently serving in the General Assembly — vied for votes alongside each other.

With only a trickle of voters heading into the senior center, sometimes the candidates made their case to the same voter at the same time or in quick succession, an odd display representing the hotly contested nature of the state Senate race.

To Karim Amin, a candidate for Democratic Central Committee who is supporting Attar, the scene at the polling place on Tuesday was encouraging, because it represents the increased interest in the 41st district.

“I’m actually kind of excited about it,” Amin said. “I’m laughing, not because I’m laughing at it — I just feel like it’s fun. They’ve been fighting so much for our community.”

Attar is ensnared in a legal battle, having been indicted in October on charges that she colluded with others to secretly film a political opponent having an affair, in order to blackmail her.

The race between Attar, a defense attorney who is the first Orthodox Jewish woman to serve in the Senate, and Ruff, a Black civil rights lawyer, has been contentious. It has also highlighted the fraught relationship between the two communities in the district, which is 63% Black, and hosts a significant Orthodox population.

“We’ve had some tough times in the past week that have highlighted the divisiveness of this race, unfortunately,” Ruff said Tuesday, as Moore stood beside him. “But what our governor represents is us bringing each other together … every creed, every religion … we have to be unified under one tent.”

In particular, Ruff took issue with a mailer recently delivered to the district from the Attar campaign, touting the fact that Moore appointed Attar to her Senate seat after a vacancy, breaking a tie at the Democratic Central Committee.

But Moore endorsed Ruff in the race, and has contributed financially to Ruff’s campaign.

“Senator Attar didn’t just earn the Governor’s trust, she’s working every day to earn yours,” the mailer reads.

“I think people see through that,” Ruff said Tuesday. “The people of our district are very astute, and so I’m hoping that the outcome will reflect that astuteness.”

Asked about the theme music that played loudly during the governor’s remarks, a bouncy tune with a snare drumbeat in the background, Ruff was lighthearted.

“I’m a soul brother,” he joked. “That ain’t my flavor.”

Whenever voters walked closer to Dr. Henry A. Wise Jr. High School in Upper Marlboro, candidates and volunteers swarmed them like bees to honey.

Among those volunteers, Eric Carpenter-Grantham walked calmly, handing voters a flyer encouraging them to choose Wanika Fisher for Prince George’s County state’s attorney.

Carpenter-Grantham and his mother, Linda, traveled from nearby Montgomery County to support Fisher.

Fisher, a former state delegate and currently a member of the Prince George’s County Council, supported one of the most popular pieces of legislation passed last year, Eric’s ID. The law allows individuals to voluntarily request a butterfly on state driver’s licenses and other forms of identification to signal to law enforcement, emergency personnel and others that the person has a hidden disability.

Carpenter-Grantham’s pink T-shirt complimented the pink Fisher campaign signs planted throughout the county.

“She’s not only a good friend of mine, [but] she is truly a warrior for P.G. County … and I pray she will be the next state’s attorney,” Eric Carpenter-Grantham said in the drizzling rain before he handed a voter a Fisher campaign flyer.
